q: When methane is chlorinated in sunlight, a small amount of ethane is found among the products. The ethane forms when:
o: Two methane molecules each lose a hydrogen atom and join
Two methyl free radicals join in a chain-termination step
A methyl free radical attacks a methane molecule
A chlorine free radical attacks a methane molecule
x: CH₃• + CH₃• → C₂H₆ is a termination step that removes two radicals. Cl• + CH₄ only gives CH₃• and HCl, and CH₃• + CH₄ just swaps a hydrogen; picking these confuses propagation with termination.

q: Propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃, is chlorinated in sunlight. Only 2 of its 8 hydrogen atoms are on the middle carbon, yet 2-chloropropane forms in about the same amount as 1-chloropropane. The best reason is that:
o: The secondary C–H bond breaks more easily, giving the more stable secondary free radical
Primary hydrogen atoms are more numerous, so they react faster
Cl⁺ ions attack the carbon atom that carries the most electrons
x: A Cl• removes a hydrogen; (CH₃)₂CH• (secondary) is more stable than CH₃CH₂CH₂• (primary), so each secondary H reacts several times faster than a primary H. Counting H atoms alone would predict 3:1 for 1-chloropropane; the reaction is free-radical, not ionic.

q: Ethene mixed with hydrogen is passed over finely divided nickel at about 250–300 °C. The product is:
x: Catalytic hydrogenation (Sabatier–Senderens) adds H₂ across C=C: CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃. Ethanol would need water, not hydrogen.

q: Iodoethane, CH₃CH₂I, is reduced with zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid. The organic product is:
x: Zn/HCl supplies hydrogen that replaces the iodine: CH₃CH₂I + 2[H] → CH₃CH₃ + HI. Butane is the Wurtz product with sodium, and ethene would need elimination with alcoholic KOH.

q: What mass of carbon dioxide is formed when 2.2 g of propane, C₃H₈, burns completely in excess oxygen? (C₃H₈ = 44, CO₂ = 44 g mol⁻¹)
x: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. 2.2/44 = 0.05 mol propane gives 0.15 mol CO₂ = 6.6 g. Forgetting the 1:3 ratio gives 2.2 g; 3.6 g is the mass of water (0.20 mol × 18).

q: 2-Bromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₃, is heated with sodium metal in dry ether (Wurtz reaction). The alkane formed is:
x: The two carbons that carried bromine join: (CH₃)₂CH–CH(CH₃)₂, named 2,3-dimethylbutane. Hexane would come from 1-bromopropane, where the chain ends join.

q: The rates at which the halogens take part in free-radical substitution of methane follow the order:
x: Reactivity falls down the group: fluorine reacts explosively, chlorine readily in light, bromine slowly, and iodine hardly at all. The reversed order mixes up reactivity with the ease of breaking the X–X bond alone.

q: One volume of a gaseous alkane needs exactly 6.5 volumes of oxygen for complete combustion, both measured at the same temperature and pressure. The alkane is:
x: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ + (3n+1)/2 O₂ → nCO₂ + (n+1)H₂O, so (3n+1)/2 = 6.5 gives n = 4 (C₄H₁₀ + 6.5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 5H₂O; O: 13 = 8 + 5). Propane needs 5 and pentane 8 volumes; forgetting that H₂O also uses oxygen gives n = 6.5, not a whole number.

q: Which compound decolourises a solution of bromine in tetrachloromethane quickly at room temperature in the dark?
x: Propene has a C=C bond and adds Br₂ at once to give 1,2-dibromopropane. The other three are saturated and react with bromine only slowly by free-radical substitution in light.

q: 2-Methylpropene, (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, reacts with HBr in the absence of peroxides. The intermediate formed in the first step is:
x: H⁺ adds to the CH₂ end so that the positive charge sits on the carbon with three alkyl groups, the most stable carbocation; Br⁻ then gives 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (Markovnikov). The free radical belongs to the peroxide route, which is excluded here.

q: 2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂, is treated with ozone and the ozonide is decomposed with zinc and water. The product is:
x: Ozonolysis cuts the C=C and puts C=O on each carbon. Each half is (CH₃)₂C=O, so two molecules of propanone form. Propanal would need an H on each double-bond carbon.

q: The reactivity of the hydrogen halides in electrophilic addition to an alkene follows the order:
x: The H–X bond gets weaker from HCl to HI, so HI gives up H⁺ to the π bond most easily. Choosing HCl first confuses bond polarity with bond strength.

q: Ethene mixed with oxygen (air) is passed over a silver catalyst at about 250 °C. The main product is:
x: Silver catalyses partial oxidation of ethene: 2CH₂=CH₂ + O₂ → 2C₂H₄O (a three-membered C–C–O ring). Ethane-1,2-diol forms with cold alkaline KMnO₄, or when epoxyethane is later hydrolysed; complete burning needs no catalyst.

q: 1,2-Dibromopropane, CH₃CHBrCH₂Br, is warmed with zinc dust in ethanol. The organic product is:
x: Zinc removes the two bromine atoms from neighbouring carbons (dehalogenation) and a C=C forms: CH₃CHBrCH₂Br + Zn → CH₃CH=CH₂ + ZnBr₂. Propyne would need two molecules of HBr removed by alcoholic KOH.

q: 5.6 g of an open-chain alkene reacts completely with exactly 16.0 g of bromine (Br = 80). Whichever way HBr adds across its double bond, the alkene can give only one structural product. The alkene is:
x: 16.0 g Br₂ = 0.10 mol, so the alkene's molar mass is 56 g mol⁻¹: C₄H₈. But-2-ene is symmetrical and gives only 2-bromobutane; but-1-ene and 2-methylpropene can each give two bromides. Propene (42) is ruled out by the mass; taking Br₂ as 80 instead of 160 gives an impossible 28 g mol⁻¹.

q: Ethene is bubbled into bromine water that also contains dissolved sodium chloride. Besides BrCH₂CH₂Br, some BrCH₂CH₂Cl is formed, but no ClCH₂CH₂Cl. This shows that:
o: Both halogen atoms add to the double bond together in a single step
Bromine oxidises Cl⁻ to Cl₂, which then adds to ethene
Bromine adds first as an electrophile, and the intermediate is then attacked by any nucleophile present, including Cl⁻
Chlorine free radicals formed from NaCl attack ethene
x: If both atoms added together, only BrCH₂CH₂Br could form. Every product has one Br, so Br⁺ adds first and the cation is then captured by Br⁻, Cl⁻ or water. Br₂ cannot oxidise Cl⁻, which is why no dichloro product appears.

q: Ethyne is mixed with excess hydrogen and passed over heated nickel. The final product is:
x: With excess H₂ both π bonds are hydrogenated: HC≡CH + 2H₂ → CH₃CH₃. Ethene is only the intermediate; stopping there needs a poisoned catalyst and one mole of H₂.

q: Ethyne reacts with one mole of hydrogen over palladium that has been partly poisoned (for example on BaSO₄ with quinoline). The main product is:
x: The poisoned catalyst is too weak to hydrogenate an alkene, so the reaction stops after one H₂ adds to the triple bond, giving CH₂=CH₂. An active nickel or platinum catalyst with excess H₂ would go on to ethane.

q: Sodium ethynide, HC≡CNa, reacts with water to form ethyne and sodium hydroxide. This shows that:
o: Ethyne is a stronger acid than water
The ethynide ion is a weaker base than the hydroxide ion
Sodium ethynide is an oxidising agent
Water is a stronger acid than ethyne
x: An acid–base reaction goes towards the weaker acid: H₂O gives H⁺ to HC≡C⁻, forming HC≡CH and OH⁻. So ethyne is the weaker acid and HC≡C⁻ the stronger base; reading the reaction backwards gives the tempting wrong option.

q: Ethyne is passed into an ammoniacal solution of copper(I) chloride. A red precipitate forms. The precipitate is:
x: The acidic hydrogens of ethyne are replaced by Cu⁺, giving red Cu–C≡C–Cu. Cu₂O is the red precipitate of the Fehling's test for aldehydes, not of alkynes.

q: 1,1,2,2-Tetrabromoethane, Br₂CHCHBr₂, is heated with excess zinc dust. The organic product is:
x: Each zinc atom removes two bromine atoms from neighbouring carbons; with excess zinc all four go and a triple bond forms: Br₂CHCHBr₂ + 2Zn → HC≡CH + 2ZnBr₂. Removing only two Br would give 1,2-dibromoethene, not ethene.

q: What volume of oxygen at STP is needed to burn 5.6 dm³ of ethyne completely? (Molar volume 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
x: 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O, so oxygen is 5/2 of the ethyne volume: 2.5 × 5.6 = 14.0 dm³. 11.2 dm³ is the CO₂ formed, and 28.0 dm³ uses the 5 without dividing by 2.

q: 1.3 g of ethyne reacts with excess bromine in tetrachloromethane until no more bromine is taken up. What mass of product forms? (C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80)
x: 1.3/26 = 0.05 mol HC≡CH. With excess bromine both π bonds add Br₂, giving CHBr₂CHBr₂ (M = 26 + 320 = 346): 0.05 × 346 = 17.3 g. Stopping at C₂H₂Br₂ (M = 186) gives 9.3 g; 8.0 g is the mass of only 0.05 mol of Br₂, not of the product.

q: Propyne, CH₃C≡CH, is hydrogenated completely with excess H₂ over nickel. The product is then chlorinated in sunlight. How many structurally different monochloro products can form?
x: Full hydrogenation gives propane, CH₃CH₂CH₃, which has two kinds of hydrogen (end CH₃ and middle CH₂), so 1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane form. Answering 3 counts each carbon separately, ignoring that the two CH₃ groups are equivalent.
